reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AASLD
clinicalPearls: A multisystem autosomal dominant disorder in which chronic cholestasis results from paucity of the interlobular bile ducts

The classic clinical constellation includes chronic cholestasis, congenital heart disease (commonly peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis), butterfly-shaped vertebral anomalies, posterior embryotoxon of the eye, and characteristic facial features
Intense pruritus and prominent xanthomas from marked hypercholesterolaemia are frequent and troublesome features
Fat malabsorption leads to failure to thrive and deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins requiring supplementation
Most cases are caused by mutations in JAG1, with a small proportion due to NOTCH2, both components of the Notch signalling pathway
Cardiac and vascular anomalies, including an increased risk of intracranial vascular events, contribute substantially to morbidity and mortality
Liver biopsy characteristically shows a reduced ratio of bile ducts to portal tracts, though duct paucity may be less evident in early infancy
Management is largely supportive, targeting pruritus, nutrition, and fat-soluble vitamins, with liver transplantation reserved for end-stage liver disease or intractable symptoms
reference.pathophysiology: Alagille syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder of the Notch signalling pathway, caused in the great majority by mutations in the JAG1 gene and less often by NOTCH2 mutations. Disrupted Notch signalling impairs normal development of the intrahepatic bile ducts, producing progressive paucity of the small interlobular ducts and consequent chronic cholestasis with retention of bile acids and cholesterol. The same signalling pathway is essential for development of the heart, vasculature, skeleton, eyes, and kidneys, which accounts for the syndrome's multisystem nature. Retained bile constituents drive pruritus and xanthoma formation, while impaired delivery of bile to the gut causes fat and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption. There is wide phenotypic variability even within families.
additionalDifferentials: Neonatal hepatitis and metabolic cholestatic disorders
Other causes of syndromic and non-syndromic bile duct paucity
additionalInvestigations: Genetic testing for JAG1 and NOTCH2 mutations to confirm the diagnosis
Echocardiography and vascular imaging for cardiac and arterial anomalies
Ophthalmological slit-lamp examination for posterior embryotoxon
Liver biopsy to demonstrate bile duct paucity when the diagnosis is unclear
Assessment of fat-soluble vitamin status and growth
redFlags: Intracranial haemorrhage or stroke from associated cerebral vascular anomalies
Severe congenital cardiac disease causing haemodynamic compromise
Progressive cholestatic liver failure and portal hypertension
Severe bleeding from vitamin K-dependent coagulopathy
reference.prognosis: Outcome is variable and depends on the severity of hepatic, cardiac, and vascular involvement; many patients survive into adulthood, but significant heart disease, progressive liver failure, and vascular events are the principal causes of mortality, and a subset require liver transplantation.
pitfalls: Relying on bile duct paucity in early infancy, when it may not yet be established, leading to misdiagnosis
Confusing the condition with biliary atresia and proceeding to unnecessary surgery
Neglecting fat-soluble vitamin supplementation and nutritional support
Overlooking the vascular and intracranial risks during interventions and anaesthesia
